challenges.name: measure-baseline-quiz
challenges.title: Is it really faster?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the CodeDev database: the same query run twice with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), and the top of a pg_stat_statements report. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

questions.question:
The course progress query was run twice in a row on the staging copy of production, right after a restart, with nothing changed in between:

-- run 1
Index Scan using lesson_progress_course_id_idx on lesson_progress  (cost=0.56..48210.33 rows=41500 width=32) (actual time=0.912..1838.207 rows=41022 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (course_id = 42)
  Buffers: shared hit=180 read=41022
Execution Time: 1843.118 ms

-- run 2
Index Scan using lesson_progress_course_id_idx on lesson_progress  (cost=0.56..48210.33 rows=41500 width=32) (actual time=0.021..95.640 rows=41022 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (course_id = 42)
  Buffers: shared hit=41202
Execution Time: 97.304 ms

Statement: "Run 2 did the same work as run 1 - the same plan touching the same 41,202 pages - and was faster only because the pages were already in shared_buffers."
questions.explanation: True. The plan, the estimate and the row count are identical, and the page count is identical too: 180 + 41,022 = 41,202 pages in run 1, 41,202 in run 2. The only difference is where the pages came from: read means PostgreSQL asked the operating system for them (from disk or from the OS page cache), hit means they were already in shared_buffers. So the 19x difference is the cache, not the query. That is why comparing a cold first run before a change with a warm second run after it proves nothing: compare runs in the same cache state, and compare the buffer counts, which do not depend on the cache.

questions.question:
The database dashboard lists the top statements from pg_stat_statements for the last 24 hours (since the last reset):

SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS mean_ms, rows, left(query, 60) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 3;

 calls  | mean_ms |  rows   | query
--------+---------+---------+--------------------------------------------------------------
     40 |  2310.0 |    1240 | SELECT c.category, count(*) FROM activity_log a JOIN courses
   1920 |    61.3 |   19200 | SELECT * FROM enrollments WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY create
 118400 |     4.2 |  118400 | SELECT id, password_hash FROM users WHERE lower(email) = $1

Statement: "The first row of this report is the statement that spent the most total time in the database during these 24 hours."
questions.explanation: False. Total time is calls x mean: 40 x 2,310 ms = 92 s for the category report, 1,920 x 61.3 ms = 118 s for the enrollments query and 118,400 x 4.2 ms = 497 s for the sign-in lookup. Ordered by mean, the sign-in query sits at the bottom although it uses five times more database time than the report at the top (pg_stat_statements also has a total_exec_time column; order by it to see the load). Mean time answers "which query is slow when it runs", total time answers "which query costs the database most" - both are worth knowing, but a ranking by mean alone hides the frequent fast query that keeps the database busy.
